title: Docker CLI Complete Reference
subtitle: A working map of every command family
description: The Docker CLI has a large but highly regular surface. Learn the grammar, the command families, and the inspection commands that answer almost every question.
outcomes: Navigate docker help and per-command help efficiently
Group commands by object and lifecycle
Use inspect, logs, stats and events as a debugging toolkit

lessons.title: CLI anatomy and help
lessons.summary: Docker commands follow a predictable grammar. Once you see it, the reference stops being intimidating.
objectives: Discover flags with --help instead of guessing

sections.title: The grammar
sections.body:
Most commands follow `docker <object> <verb> [options] [target]`. Management commands group verbs: `docker container ls`, `docker image rm`, `docker network inspect`. Shorthands exist for daily use: `docker ps` = `docker container ls`, `docker images` = `docker image ls`, `docker rmi` = `docker image rm`.

Global options come before the command (`--context`, `--host`, `--log-level`, `-H`). Command options come after the verb.

sections.code:
docker --help
docker container --help
docker run --help
docker compose --help
docker compose up --help
sections.note: The --help output in OpsDeck is read live from your installed CLI, so flags always match your engine version.

sections.title: Use --format for machines, tables for humans
sections.body: Most list commands accept `--format` with Go templates and `{{json .}}` for JSON lines. That is how OpsDeck reads your engine without parsing tables.

lessons.title: Container lifecycle commands
lessons.summary: The complete set of verbs that move a container from created to removed.
objectives: Choose between run, create, start and exec

sections.title: Create is not start
sections.body:
`docker create` builds a container and its writable layer without starting it. `docker start` starts an existing container. `docker run` is create + start. This matters for orchestration and for restarting a configured container without losing its layer.

`docker exec` runs an additional process inside a running container. It is not a lifecycle command and does not restart or replace the main process.

sections.code:
docker create --name worker -e MODE=batch alpine sleep 3600
docker start worker
docker exec -it worker sh
docker pause worker && docker unpause worker
docker stop worker
docker rm worker

docker cp ./config.json worker:/app/config.json
docker inspect worker --format '{{.State.Status}} {{.State.ExitCode}}'
sections.note: Stopping sends SIGTERM, waits (`--time`, default 10s), then SIGKILL. Handle SIGTERM in your app for graceful shutdown.

head: Verb
Effect
rows: Start or gracefully stop an existing container
Freeze or resume processes with the freezer cgroup
Run an extra process in a running container
Remove a stopped container (use -f to force)

sections.title: docker attach is rarely what you want
sections.body: Attaching to PID 1 means Ctrl-C can kill the container. Use `docker exec -it` for shells unless you are deliberately attaching to a TUI process.

lessons.title: Image and system commands
lessons.summary: Inspect, transfer, clean and measure images without guessing.
objectives: Inspect image metadata and layer history

sections.title: Inspection before deletion
sections.body: `docker image inspect` exposes config, environment, entrypoint, labels and digests. `docker image history` shows the layers and the commands that created them — invaluable for finding accidental secrets or oversized layers.

sections.code:
docker image ls --digests
docker image inspect nginx:alpine --format '{{.Config.Entrypoint}} {{.Config.Cmd}}'
docker image history nginx:alpine
docker image save -o nginx.tar nginx:alpine
docker image load -i nginx.tar

docker system df
docker image prune -a
docker system prune --volumes
sections.output:
TYPE            TOTAL     ACTIVE    SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          107       10        101.4GB   61.28GB (60%)
sections.note: `docker system prune --volumes` removes unused volumes too. Read the confirmation prompt; it is not recoverable.

sections.title: Prune is destructive
sections.body: `docker system prune -a --volumes` removes every unused image, network, build cache and volume. Back up named volumes first.

questions.question: Which command shows the layers of an image?
questions.explain: image history lists layers and their creating commands.

questions.question: How do you move an image to an offline host?

questions.question: Which prune removes unused volumes?
